title: India's AI.
Your Edge.
redrob-llm.brief: Led end-to-end UX design of Redrob AI — India's first conversational intelligence workspace. Designed a natural-language search interface, a modular AI App Store with 14 apps, a Contacts CRM, AI agent-powered Chat Rooms, and a Projects layer — all built on Redrob 2B, the company's proprietary LLM serving India's most ambitious recruiters, sales professionals, and job seekers.

cover.label: Redrob AI — India's AI. Your Edge.

context.h: India had the world's 3rd-largest talent pool with no intelligence platform built for it.
context.b: India's startup ecosystem crossed 100,000+ registered companies, with hundreds of thousands of active recruiters and B2B sales teams. Yet every intelligence tool — LinkedIn, Apollo, Crunchbase — was built for Silicon Valley workflows, priced in dollars, and largely blind to India-specific company and professional data. Redrob's founding thesis: build a conversational AI workspace that treats India as the primary market, not an afterthought, and serves every user — from senior recruiter to fresh graduate — with one natural language interface powered by a proprietary LLM (Redrob 2B).

research.h: 56 sessions across 4 user types. The tool-switching tax was universal — but the need was deeply personal.
research.b: Over an 8-week discovery sprint, I ran 56 research sessions spanning 4 distinct user types: recruiters, B2B sales reps (SDRs), job seekers, and founder-researchers. I used in-depth interviews, contextual inquiry sessions observing live workflows, competitive teardowns of 12 tools, and diary studies. The defining insight wasn't a feature gap — it was a positioning gap. India's most ambitious professionals had no platform designed with their context, their companies, and their cities in mind.

bullets.v: Recruiters, SDRs, job seekers, founders across 8 Indian cities
Observed live search and outreach workflows across all 4 user types
LinkedIn, Apollo, Naukri, Crunchbase, Lusha, Hunter, Glassdoor & more
Tool satisfaction, switching frequency, and unmet needs across India

insights: The average recruiter switched between 4.3 tools per candidate search — costing 7–11 minutes per lookup. Users weren't slow; their toolstack was broken.
Indian company and professional data was absent or inaccurate on global tools. 68% of users reported finding a contact record outdated in the past week.
Job seekers wanted intelligence, not listings — they wanted to know which companies were actually hiring, who to reach, and what to say to them.

Every user — from senior recruiter to fresh graduate — wanted to type a question in plain language and get a direct answer. Filter-heavy search forms felt like operating a machine, not having a conversation.

goals: Find qualified Indian talent by natural language description
Rank and shortlist without building a manual spreadsheet
Track all sourcing and outreach from a single place
pains: LinkedIn searches India poorly — wrong cities, wrong company sizes
Contact data expires fast — phone numbers wrong 40% of the time
No way to compare 3 candidates side-by-side without leaving the tool

personas.name: Arjun Mehta
personas.role: Sales Development Representative, B2B SaaS Company
personas.quote: My entire job is finding the right person at the right company and saying the right thing. I need all three to happen in under 30 seconds.
goals: Find decision-makers at target companies by role and seniority
Get verified email and phone with company context attached
Build targeted outreach lists with one search, not five tools
pains: Apollo has poor India coverage — most leads are outdated or wrong
Company context and contact are always on different screens

personas.name: Kavya Rao

pains: Job portals are flooded with stale, low-quality listings
No visibility into real hiring velocity at a specific company
No guidance on how to approach, who to contact, or what to say

problem.h: Reframed from 'India's LinkedIn' to 'India's AI that gives you unfair knowledge'.
problem.b: The initial brief was to build a better LinkedIn for India. Research reframed it entirely. The real gap wasn't another profile directory — it was a conversational intelligence layer that unified people, company, and job data under one natural-language interface, trained on Indian professional context. This reframe changed everything: the primary interaction model shifted from filters and forms to conversation. The design challenge became — how do you make a complex data platform feel as simple as texting a colleague who knows everything?
problem.statement: How might we design a conversational AI workspace — with natural language as its primary interface — that gives India's most ambitious professionals instant, contextual access to people, company, and job intelligence, and makes them feel like the smartest person in any room?

journey.h: From query to action in one flow — no tab switching, no manual enrichment.
journey.b: I mapped three parallel journeys for the recruiter, the SDR, and the job seeker. They shared the same core architecture — intent → search → enrich → act → collaborate — but diverged sharply in what 'acting' meant. This informed a key architectural decision: a unified search layer with user-type-aware result cards. Each user type sees the same interface but receives context optimised for their intent.

phases.name: Intent
tasks: Select mode chip: People / Company / Jobs
phases.pain: Early testing showed users didn't know what syntax worked — the LLM had to infer intent from ambiguous, casual phrasing

phases.name: Search
phases.pain: Result relevance varied by query type — required significant LLM tuning cycles based on user feedback

phases.name: Enrich
tasks: View profile with role, company, location
phases.pain: Users wanted to preview result quality before spending contact unlock credits — no-preview model caused credit anxiety

phases.name: Act
phases.pain: Action felt disconnected — users left the platform to act on what they found, losing all context

phases.name: Collaborate
tasks: Ask AI agent (Finn, Pixel, Memo, Draft) for next step
Build persistent Project with memory across sessions
phases.pain: No team-sharing model meant every recruiter and sales rep was working in isolation — findings couldn't compound

process.h: 14 sprints. 3 major pivots. One live platform — and a design system built to scale.
process.b: The design process ran across 14 two-week sprints over 8 months in 4 phases. Phase 1 established the core conversational search interface and intent chip model. Phase 2 designed the AI App Store architecture. Phase 3 built Chat Rooms with named AI agents. Phase 4 shipped the Contacts CRM and Projects layer. Three major design pivots emerged from testing: the move from tab navigation to intent chips; the App Store model replacing a monolithic feature set; and named AI agents (Finn, Pixel, Memo, Draft) replacing a generic assistant interface. Each pivot was driven by user testing, not opinion.

artifacts.v: 6-icon sidebar with progressive disclosure — tested against top-nav and full-sidebar in 3 rounds
Natural language input with People / Company / Jobs chips replacing all filter forms
Modular, activatable apps — 7 live at launch (People Search, Company Search, Job Search, Resume Ranker, Drive, Gmail, Calendar) + 7 on roadmap
4 distinct agents with bounded scopes: Finn (finance), Pixel (UI/UX), Memo (meeting notes), Draft (content writing)
Auto-populated from every search session — Grade A contact filtering, phone unlock, LinkedIn sync
Dark-mode first, 80+ components, IBM Plex Serif brand typeface, full token architecture

solution.h: A conversational intelligence workspace where India's professionals know everything.
solution.b: The shipped product is a multi-surface AI workspace built on Redrob 2B, the company's own proprietary LLM. Natural language search with intent chips replaced filter-heavy forms. An AI App Store lets users activate only the modules they need — from People Search to Gmail to Calendar — keeping the experience uncluttered. Chat Rooms give teams a collaborative space with named AI agents as specialised members. The Contacts CRM auto-populates from every search interaction, creating a living professional network. Projects give persistent memory across sessions. Redrob GTM (700M+ profiles) and Redrob Signal (AI-powered IPL predictions, Android) extend the platform beyond the browser.
highlights: Conversational search with intent chips — type in plain language, tag it as People / Company / Job. Redrob 2B infers context and returns direct, enriched answers — no filters, no forms.

AI App Store — 14 modular apps all powered by one LLM. Users activate only what they need: People Search, Company Search, Job Search, Resume Ranker (PRO), Drive, Gmail, Calendar, and 7 more on the roadmap including Interview Coach, Skill Tests, and VC-PE Scout.

Chat Rooms with named AI agents — Finn handles budget and finance queries, Pixel reviews design decisions, Memo summarises meeting threads and creates action items, Draft writes and improves any content. AI feels like a specialist colleague, not a generic chatbot.
Auto-populated Contacts CRM — every profile searched or unlocked flows automatically into a structured CRM with Grade A contact filtering, phone unlock credits, and LinkedIn badges.

Projects — persistent, contextual workspaces for ongoing tasks. Pre-built templates for Investing, Writing, Homework, and Travel reduce setup friction and make the LLM context-aware from the first session.

outcomes.h: 700M+ profiles. 14 apps at launch. India's first conversational intelligence platform, live.

metrics.sub: Searchable via natural language query at launch
7 live at launch · 7 on the product roadmap

quote.q: Redrob feels like someone finally built a professional tool for India — not a Western product with Indian data bolted on, but something built from the ground up for how we actually work.
quote.a: Early user, Sales Lead at a Bangalore B2B startup

reflection.h: The most important design decision was what we chose not to show.
reflection.b: The App Store model began as an engineering architecture decision — but became the most important UX decision on the entire product. By letting users activate only the apps they needed, we eliminated the onboarding paralysis that comes with capability-rich platforms, and dramatically improved first-session task completion rates. I'd apply this progressive capability disclosure principle to every multi-feature platform I design going forward. The second major learning: AI agents need names, personalities, and narrow scopes. When Finn 'handles budget queries' and Pixel 'reviews design decisions,' users form clear mental models and use them confidently and repeatedly. A generic 'AI assistant' gets ignored. Specificity is the whole game.

title: Creatives that
convert at scale.
phot-ai.brief: Led end-to-end product design for Phot AI — a Creative-Led Growth Platform for D2C and e-commerce brands. Designed three flagship modules — AngleLab (signal-based ad creative generation), ListingLab (AI marketplace listing optimisation), and VideoLab (performance video production) — plus a 5-agent AI architecture, reducing creative cycles from 2 weeks to same-day and delivering +47% average ROAS uplift.

context.h: Ad creatives were decaying 47% in CTR within 2 weeks — and every brand was guessing why.
context.b: D2C and e-commerce brands face a brutal creative reality: ad creatives decay fast (-47% CTR after 2 weeks on average), 87% of tested angles fail, and the average brand spends 5+ hours manually producing a single marketplace listing. Agencies promise solutions but run on intuition, not signal. Phot AI was founded on a different thesis — creative decisions should be driven by data, not guesses. The product's job: build a system that turns product inputs into campaign-ready creatives, tested against real performance signals, at a speed no human team can match.

research.h: 26 brands. The problem wasn't creative quality — it was creative intelligence.
research.b: Over a 6-week discovery sprint, I ran 26 in-depth interviews across D2C founders, performance marketing managers, creative directors, and e-commerce operators; 10 workflow shadowing sessions tracking live creative production cycles end-to-end; and a competitive teardown of 14 tools. The dominant finding: brands weren't producing bad creatives. They were producing creatives without knowing which angles would actually work — and by the time they had signal, the ads were already fatigued.

bullets.v: Founders, performance marketers, creative leads, e-com operators
Tracked full creative cycle: brief → shoot → edit → publish → iterate
Canva, Adobe Firefly, Midjourney, DALL·E, Pencil, Smartly, Predis & more
Creative production time, cost, angle testing frequency, ROAS trends

insights: 87% of creative angles brands test fail — not because the product is bad, but because angle selection is based on gut feel, not competitive signal data.
Creative fatigue is the #1 silent ROAS killer: CTR drops 47% on average within 2 weeks, but most brands only notice when ROAS has already declined 32%.
Performance marketers — not designers — are the primary users. The interface had to work for someone who can't distinguish a hex code from a font weight.
Listing quality on Amazon/Shopify was bleeding conversion silently: 1:1 listings-to-format ratio, unoptimised titles, and A+ content taking 5+ hours per SKU to produce manually.

personas.role: Performance Marketing Manager, D2C Beauty Brand

goals: Produce optimised Amazon listings at scale
Improve search visibility and add-to-cart rates
Generate A+ content without a copywriter or designer
pains: Manual listing production: 5+ hours per SKU
PDP traffic landing but not converting (2.3% avg CVR)
No system — every listing is a one-off effort

personas.name: Meera Joshi

Connect creative decisions to actual revenue signal
pains: Canva doesn't understand performance

No brand memory — re-brief every session, no consistency

problem.h: Reframed from 'AI photo editor' to 'creative intelligence engine that closes the signal loop'.
problem.b: The original brief: a faster AI image editor. Research reframed it completely. Brands didn't need prettier images — they needed smarter angle selection, faster creative iteration, and a closed loop between creative output and performance signal. The design challenge became: how do you make a complex intelligence system feel as simple as uploading a product photo? And how do you surface performance data in a way that a non-analyst can act on in under 60 seconds?
problem.statement: How might we design a creative growth platform that uses competitive signal and performance data to automatically generate, test, and surface winning ad angles — so D2C brands stop guessing and start compounding?

journey.h: From product URL to campaign-ready creatives, guided by signal — not guesswork.
journey.b: I mapped the end-to-end journey for a performance marketer — from inputting a product to deploying validated creatives. The critical insight from journey mapping: the biggest drop-off wasn't in production, it was in the gap between creative output and performance feedback. Brands produced creatives, published them, waited 2 weeks, then started over. The platform needed to collapse that loop.

phases.name: Input
tasks: Upload product image or paste listing URL
System auto-extracts attributes, audience context, category benchmarks
phases.pain: Manual briefing was inconsistent — different marketers described the same product in completely different ways

phases.name: Discover
tasks: AI analyses top-performing creatives in your category
Generates ranked angles mapped to your ICP
Surfaces 12+ testable angles with predicted performance scores
phases.pain: Angle selection had always been subjective — marketers were uncomfortable trusting a ranked list they couldn't verify

phases.name: Generate
tasks: AngleLab produces static, video, carousel, and story variants
ListingLab creates Amazon/Shopify titles, bullets, A+ content
VideoLab generates video ads with AI CMO and Creative Strategist agents
phases.pain: Output quality varied by product category — reflective surfaces and food photography were consistently harder

phases.name: Review
tasks: Brand consistency check against stored guidelines
phases.pain: No collaboration layer meant review happened over WhatsApp screenshots — context was always lost

phases.name: Deploy
tasks: System flags fatigue and surfaces next angle to test
phases.pain: Post-publish performance data never fed back into the creative process — every new brief started from zero

process.h: 5 sprints. Tested with live brand assets and real campaign data — not stock photos.
process.b: I ran 5 two-week design sprints, each producing a testable prototype. A non-negotiable rule: every usability test used participants' actual product images and real campaign data, not generic photos. This immediately surfaced the edge cases that matter — complex backgrounds, multi-product shots, reflective packaging, lifestyle images. Five rounds, 40 participants, 220 tasks logged. Two critical pivots emerged: the Angle Discovery interface required a transparent score explanation to build trust, and the listing editor needed a side-by-side 'before/after' view to make AI edits defensible to clients.

artifacts.v: AngleLab / ListingLab / VideoLab — 3 distinct modules, 1 unified system
Ranked angles with signal source explanations — built for non-analyst trust
5 agents: AI CMO, Creative Strategist, VideoLab, Copywriting, Human Review
Side-by-side before/after with SEO score, readability grade, CVR prediction
In-platform review with threaded comments, approval states, version history
60+ components, dark + light modes, optimised for data-dense dashboards

solution.h: Three engines. One platform. Signal-driven creative from input to outcome.
solution.b: The shipped platform has three flagship modules. AngleLab: input a product, get 12+ ranked ad angles derived from real competitive signal — not guesses. ListingLab: AI-generated Amazon and Shopify listings (titles, bullets, A+ content) produced in minutes not days, with SEO optimisation and CVR scoring built in. VideoLab: AI-produced video ads powered by a 5-agent pipeline (AI CMO Agent, Creative Strategist, VideoLab Agent, AI Copywriting Agent, and Human Review for final QA). The platform also offers a fully-managed AI Agency tier for brands that want outcomes without touching the tools.
highlights: AngleLab — AI analyses your category's top-performing creatives, generates 12+ ranked angles mapped to your ICP, and flags fatigue so you always have the next test ready.
ListingLab — Amazon and Shopify listings generated at scale: titles, bullets, A+ content, and 8+ product photos, cutting production from 5+ hours to minutes per SKU.
VideoLab — AI CMO Agent defines positioning, AI Creative Strategist writes hooks, VideoLab Agent produces visuals, AI Copywriting Agent writes the script, Human Review finalises quality.
Signal Closed Loop — performance data from live campaigns feeds back into Angle Discovery, making every cycle faster and more accurate than the last.
Dual delivery model — SaaS for teams who want control, fully-managed AI Agency for brands who want outcomes with no operational lift.

quote.q: We went from 2-week creative cycles to same-day iteration. Our design workflow is dramatically faster and more efficient.
quote.a: Nikhil Jain, Founder, Behoma — Phot AI customer

reflection.h: The hardest design problem wasn't the AI — it was making machine intelligence feel trustworthy.
reflection.b: The biggest UX challenge on this project wasn't generating creatives — it was convincing performance marketers to trust an AI-ranked angle list over their own intuition. The pivot that unlocked adoption: every ranked angle now shows its signal source (competitor analysis, ICP match score, historical performance data). Once users could interrogate the reasoning, they stopped overriding the AI and started testing it. The learning I carry forward: on any AI product, explainability is not a nice-to-have — it is the trust mechanism that determines whether users adopt or abandon the intelligent recommendation. Build that layer first.

title: Cricket meets
celebrity culture.
bcl.brief: Designed the complete digital experience for India's first celebrity cricket league — a live platform serving 6 celebrity-owned teams, 90+ real-time statistics, dynamic leaderboards, fan prediction games, and an identity system for each team. The core challenge: one app serving hardcore cricket statisticians and casual celebrity fans simultaneously without alienating either.

cover.label: Big Celebrity League — Where Cricket Meets Celebrity Culture

context.h: India has 600M+ cricket fans and an equally intense celebrity culture. BCL was the first league to merge both.
context.b: The Big Celebrity League is India's first-of-its-kind format: 6 cricket teams owned and represented by Bollywood actors, musicians, and social media stars, competing in a live structured tournament. The product challenge was unprecedented — designing a live cricket experience that served two audiences with almost opposite consumption patterns: hardcore cricket fans who demand ball-by-ball data density, and celebrity fans who follow for moments, drama, and their favourite star's face. Most platforms choose one. BCL had to serve both.

research.h: 38 interviews. Two audiences with opposite mental models of what 'following cricket' means.
research.b: I ran a 5-week research sprint: 38 in-depth interviews across 3 audience types (hardcore cricket fans, celebrity followers, and casual sports viewers), 6 live diary studies during a BCL pilot match tracking real-time in-app behaviour and emotional states, competitive analysis of 10 sports and entertainment apps, and a card-sorting exercise with 45 participants on stat priority and content preference.

bullets.v: Hardcore cricket fans, celebrity followers, casual viewers across 6 cities
Real-time emotional and behavioural tracking during BCL pilot match
Cricbuzz, Dream11, Hotstar, Fancam, NBA, IPL app, Fancode & more
Stat priority and content preference mapping with both audience types

insights: Cricket fans treat stats as respect — omitting wagon wheels, economy rates, or partnership data signals that the app 'doesn't take cricket seriously.' Data density is emotional, not just informational.
Celebrity fans don't follow the sport — they follow the person. They want close-up moments, reactions, personality, and something shareable to Instagram within 10 seconds of it happening.
Score update latency is a trust signal: if scores don't update within 30 seconds, both audiences assume the app is broken and switch. Perceived real-time is non-negotiable.
Prediction and participation mechanics drove significantly longer session times for casual fans — they stayed not to watch, but to compete and be right.

personas.name: Rahul Verma
personas.quote: I need ball-by-ball, run rate, wagon wheel, partnership stats. If your app doesn't have all of that, I'll keep Cricbuzz open in the other tab.
goals: Ball-by-ball live accuracy with under 15s latency
Full innings data: economy, strike rate, partnerships, wagon wheel
Compare BCL player performance against IPL and domestic cricket stats
pains: Celebrity apps historically treat stats as decoration, not data
Score delays of even 60 seconds feel like the app has crashed
No context for celebrity players — hard to evaluate performance without career baseline

personas.name: Neha Sharma
personas.quote: I'm here because my favourite actor is playing. I want to see him bat, see his team, follow his journey in the tournament. Not 7 tabs of cricket statistics.
goals: Team page dedicated to her favourite celebrity with content feed and match stats
Shareable highlights — a video clip or moment card in under 5 seconds
Tournament narrative — who's winning, what's the drama, what happened this week
pains: Standard cricket interfaces are jargon-heavy and visually intimidating
No celebrity-specific content — just generic match data
Can't share moments natively — forced to screenshot and lose visual quality

personas.name: Karan Malhotra
personas.role: Casual Sports Fan & Social Predictor, 31, Pune
personas.quote: I don't know the players well but BCL feels like entertainment. If there's a prediction game I can win, I'll stay all match.
goals: Quick glance understanding of match state — who's winning, what's the score
Prediction mechanic that makes watching feel participatory
Share prediction performance and tournament leaderboard on WhatsApp groups
pains: Standard cricket scorecards overwhelm him with data he can't contextualise
No low-stakes entry point for someone who's interested but not obsessed
No way to stay engaged between overs or between matches

problem.h: The architecture had to serve two mentally incompatible audiences without building two apps.
problem.b: The core tension: cricket fans wanted maximum data density by default; celebrity fans wanted maximum visual storytelling by default. A single middle-ground screen would satisfy neither. The design breakthrough came from separating the question of default state from the question of available depth. The default experience would be visually rich and emotionally driven — optimised for the majority casual audience. Statistical depth would be available one tap deeper, always — optimised for the minority hardcore audience who'd seek it out regardless.
problem.statement: How might we design a live cricket platform that makes hardcore fans feel like they have a statistician's toolkit, casual fans feel like they're watching reality TV, and celebrity fans feel like they're in the front row — all at the same time?

journey.h: From match-day notification to post-match story share — 5 emotional states, 5 interface modes.
journey.b: I mapped the fan journey across the full arc of a live match day — pre-match anticipation, live match tension, milestone moments (sixes, wickets, partnerships), post-match debrief, and inter-match engagement between tournament fixtures. Each emotional state required a different interface mode and different content hierarchy. The journey made it clear: the app couldn't be a static scorecard — it had to shift personality as the match progressed.

phases.name: Pre-Match
tasks: Check team lineup and injury updates
Browse celebrity team page and tournament standings
phases.pain: No anticipation mechanics — nothing to do before the first ball. Users opened the app and closed it immediately.

phases.name: Live
tasks: Celebrity player highlight feed alongside scoreboard
Live chat and reactions with other fans
phases.pain: The two data streams (cricket stats + celebrity content) competed for the same screen space — early designs felt cluttered and unfocused.

phases.name: Milestones
tasks: Auto-generated moment card on every 6, 4, wicket, and milestone
Celebrity reaction capture and highlight clip
Instant share to Instagram Story / WhatsApp
phases.pain: Moments passed before users could react. If the share flow took more than 3 taps, the moment was already irrelevant by the time it was shared.

phases.name: Post-Match
tasks: Updated tournament standings and points table
phases.pain: Post-match data was scattered across 3 tabs. Users who wanted a complete picture had to navigate — and most dropped off before finding everything.

phases.name: Inter-Match
tasks: Check tournament standings and team news
Complete prediction challenges for upcoming fixtures
Browse celebrity team content between matches
phases.pain: Between matches, there was no reason to open the app. Retention between fixtures was the biggest unsolved gap.

process.h: 6 scorecard iterations. Prototype-tested during a live match. One breakthrough pivot.
process.b: The design process had one constraint that changed everything: we ran prototype tests during an actual BCL pilot match — with real users, real live data, and the genuine emotional stakes of a match in progress. This was irreplaceable. We discovered that cognitive load spikes dramatically during a live six or wicket moment — and any interface complexity at that point causes complete disengagement. We iterated the scorecard 6 times, the team page 4 times, and the moment-share flow 5 times. The key pivot: replacing a persistent navigation bar (which users ignored during play) with a gesture-based mode-switch that kept the live data screen completely uninterrupted.

artifacts.v: Live (stats-dense) / Fan (celeb-content-led) / Compete (prediction) — tested against 5-tab and 2-tab alternatives
Summary glance (match state, key wickets) → full innings detail → player career comparison
Custom colour systems, mascots, typographic treatments — each team visually distinct at a glance
Auto-triggered on every 6, 4, wicket, milestone — with team branding, player photo, and stat snapshot
Pre-match winner, over-by-over runs, individual performance — points, streaks, tournament leaderboard
Moment card → personalised with team colour → directly to Instagram/WhatsApp in one action

solution.h: One platform. Three modes. Every type of fan feels like it was built for them.
solution.b: The final product is structured around three engagement modes that users move between naturally during a match. Live Mode delivers stat density on demand — progressive scorecard with full innings data, run rate, economy, wagon wheel, and ball-by-ball commentary. Fan Mode centres the celebrity team identity — team page, player highlights, tournament narrative, and fan community. Compete Mode turns watching into participating — prediction games, streak tracking, and a tournament-wide leaderboard. The moment-share system auto-generates branded cards for every significant event, shareable to any platform in a single tap.
highlights: Progressive scorecard — glanceable match state at default view, expands to full ball-by-ball innings detail, economy, wagon wheel, and career comparison on demand.
6 celebrity team identities — each team has its own colour system, mascot, and dedicated content feed. Following a team feels like following a person.
Auto-triggered Moment Cards — a branded, shareable card is generated within 3 seconds of every six, four, wicket, or milestone. One tap to Instagram or WhatsApp.
Prediction Engine — ball-level and match-level predictions with a persistent tournament leaderboard. Streaks, badges, and ranking drive daily opens between matches.
Gesture-based mode switching — no persistent navigation bar cluttering the live screen. A single swipe shifts between Live, Fan, and Compete without breaking immersion.

outcomes.h: 6 teams. 90+ live stats. 62% ops cost saved. Fans stayed for the full 20 overs.

quote.q: As a hardcore cricket fan, I genuinely didn't expect to love a celebrity league app. But the live data depth is actually better than some mainstream cricket apps I use daily.
quote.a: Beta user, cricket fan, Delhi — Season 1 feedback

reflection.h: When two audiences conflict, test — don't debate. Data will tell you who to prioritise.
reflection.b: The defining decision: default to data density or visual storytelling? My instinct was visual — most users are casual. The A/B test on the pilot group said data-dense views had 34% longer session times across all user types, including casual fans. The data-dense default won. The insight: casual fans don't need simpler interfaces — they need better progressive disclosure. Lead with what engaged users want, and make the simple path obvious for everyone else. I'd also tackle inter-match retention much earlier next time — the biggest engagement gap was the 6-day silence between fixtures, and we had no designed solution for it.

title: 80 years of
legacy, reimagined.
pritam.brief: Led the end-to-end digital redesign of Pritam Restaurant — Mumbai's first Punjabi eatery, established in 1947 and credited with introducing Butter Chicken to the city. Designed a storytelling-first website and reservation system that preserved the restaurant's slow-cooking philosophy and 76-year reputation while opening it to a new generation of diners — without a single compromise on authenticity.

context.h: Mumbai's oldest Punjabi kitchen had no website, no reservations system, and a 76-year story told to no one.
context.b: Pritam Restaurant opened in Chembur, Mumbai in 1947 — and by most accounts, brought Butter Chicken to the city for the first time. Three generations of the Kohli family had sustained it through reputation alone: no website, no online reservations, no digital presence. In 2023, Abhiraj Kohli — the third-generation owner — came to us with a deceptively simple brief: 'Help people find us and book a table. But don't make it feel like we changed.' The real challenge was more nuanced. Pritam's legacy was its identity. If the digital experience felt modern, clean, or generic, it would signal something false. If it felt too archival, it wouldn't convert a first-time visitor who'd never heard of the place. The design had to earn trust from two completely opposite audiences simultaneously.

research.h: 28 conversations. Two audiences with opposite fears — both united by the food.
research.b: I ran a 3-week discovery phase: 28 interviews split between long-term regulars (some with 20+ years of visits) and younger, first-time visitors. I also conducted a full-service observation day at the restaurant, analysed 300+ Google, Zomato, and TripAdvisor reviews for sentiment patterns, and audited 14 heritage restaurant digital presences across India, the UK, and the US to find global benchmarks. The starkest finding: both audiences had a fear — and both fears were legitimate.

bullets.v: 16 long-term regulars (10+ year visitors) + 12 younger first-time or prospective visitors
Google Business, Zomato, TripAdvisor — thematic coding for praise, friction, and unmet expectations
Restaurant digital experiences from India, UK, US — identifying what preserves and what dilutes identity
Observed peak service: walk-in flow, ordering rituals, how regulars interacted with staff vs. new visitors

insights: Long-term regulars' #1 fear: 'modernising' would signal price hikes, changed recipes, or loss of the honest, no-frills character that made Pritam what it is. The word 'redesign' was a threat.

First-time visitors discovered Pritam through word of mouth, but without an online booking option, they switched to restaurants that could be booked on Zomato. Pritam lost them at the decision moment.

The Butter Chicken origin story — that Pritam is credited with bringing Butter Chicken to Mumbai — was known internally but communicated nowhere. It was the single most emotionally powerful piece of content the brand had, and it was invisible.
Menu discovery was the top pre-visit need: 71% of younger visitors wanted to browse the menu before committing to a visit, and not finding one was a conversion-killer.

personas.name: Vijay Bhatt
personas.role: Retired professional, 62, a Pritam regular since 1981
personas.quote: I've been coming here for 40 years. The dal makhani recipe hasn't changed once. I hope the website doesn't make it look like it has.
goals: Check today's specials without calling
Book a table for family milestones
Show younger relatives 'where I grew up eating'
pains: Fears modernisation signals something changed
Not digitally confident — complex forms are a barrier
Worried the 'character' gets designed away

personas.name: Ananya Mehta
personas.quote: My colleague said Pritam invented Butter Chicken in Mumbai. I looked it up — found nothing. I went somewhere I could book instead.
goals: Browse full menu with photos before visiting
Book a table instantly online
Understand the story — heritage sells to my audience
pains: No digital presence = no trust for new visitors
Can't book = chooses a competitor who can
No photos of food or ambience to assess

personas.name: Abhiraj Kohli
personas.quote: My grandfather slow-cooked this into what it is. My job is to make sure the next generation finds it — without losing what made it worth finding.
goals: Bring younger diners through the door
Eliminate overbooking via a proper reservation system
Tell the 76-year story with the pride it deserves
pains: Fears a 'generic' website will misrepresent 76 years of character
Paper reservation book causes double-bookings and missed tables
No mechanism to capture contacts for events or special occasions

problem.h: Reframed from 'build a website' to 'make 76 years of character feel alive, not archived'.
problem.b: The easy brief was: build a restaurant website with a menu and a booking form. Research completely reframed it. The real challenge was a dual-trust problem. New visitors needed to trust that a walk-in would be worth it — they needed the story, the food photography, the social proof. Long-term regulars needed to trust that nothing had changed — that the website was a window into the same Pritam, not a replacement for it. These two trust needs pulled in opposite directions aesthetically. The wrong design would alienate one audience. The right design had to speak to both.
problem.statement: How might we build a digital presence for Pritam that makes first-time visitors excited to discover a 76-year institution — and makes long-term regulars proud rather than worried — without the design contradicting the restaurant's slow-cooking, no-frills soul?

journey.h: From Zomato search to reserved table — without losing a single visitor to a competitor.
journey.b: I mapped the discovery-to-visit journey for both a new visitor and a returning regular. The most critical insight: the journeys diverged completely at discovery and evaluation, but converged at the reservation step. The implication for design was structural: the hero and story sections had to be built for conversion of first-time visitors (who needed to trust the place was real and special), while the reservation flow needed to be designed with the regulars' digital confidence level as the floor — simple, forgiving, and immediately confirmable.

phases.name: Discover
phases.pain: No website, no Zomato listing optimised — lost to competitors on first Google page

phases.name: Evaluate
phases.pain: No menu online, no food photography — 71% of new visitors needed both before committing

phases.name: Trust
phases.pain: Butter Chicken origin story — Pritam's single biggest differentiator — was communicated nowhere

phases.name: Reserve
phases.pain: Phone-only booking — new visitors hung up; regulars often found the line busy

phases.name: Visit
tasks: Order from a menu they recognise
phases.pain: No post-visit digital touchpoint — no review prompt, no loyalty mechanism, no way to reconnect

process.h: Three visual directions. Tested at the restaurant, between service periods, on regulars' phones.
process.b: The research constraint was unusual and clarifying: I tested high-fidelity prototypes with actual long-term regulars at Pritam — over chai, between the lunch and dinner service rush. This meant designs had to work on older Android devices, in warm dim restaurant lighting, with users who were not digitally confident. I tested 3 visual directions (heritage-forward, contemporary-minimal, hybrid), 2 navigation structures, and 4 iterations of the reservation flow. The heritage-forward direction won comprehensively — not just for older regulars, but for younger visitors too, who responded to the authenticity as a point of differentiation.

artifacts.v: Heritage design language — deep reds, aged patina textures, hand-drawn recipe-card typography, archival family photography
Photo-led, category-first menu — every signature dish photographed with portions, price, and heritage context note
76-year decade-by-decade timeline — founding, the Butter Chicken moment, generational handovers, media milestones
4-step booking — date, party size, contact, WhatsApp confirmation. No account creation. Works on any device.
83% of discovery traffic was mobile — designed entirely mobile-up, desktop as secondary
'Butter Chicken origin' and 'Mumbai's first Punjabi restaurant' as anchor content — targeting heritage and food interest search

solution.h: Heritage surfaced. Story told. Table booked in 4 steps.
solution.b: The final design was built on three pillars working simultaneously. Storytelling first: the hero opened with the Butter Chicken origin claim, supported by decade-by-decade visual history, family photography, and media mentions — giving first-time visitors immediate context for why this restaurant was different. Menu discovery second: a full photo-led menu with clear portions, legacy notes on signature dishes, and category filters for dietary needs. Reservation third: a 4-step booking flow requiring only name, date, party size, and phone — confirmation via WhatsApp, no account, no friction. The visual language used archival warmth throughout — the deep reds of a Punjabi kitchen, the weight of hand-set type, the imperfection of aged textures — without ever feeling like a costume.
highlights: Butter Chicken origin as hero content — led with Pritam's claim to fame, the single most differentiating story the brand had.
76-year heritage timeline — decade-by-decade visual history with family photographs, media coverage, and generational milestones.
Photo-led menu — every signature dish photographed with portion size, legacy context, and price clearly visible.
4-step reservation flow — name, date, party, WhatsApp confirm. No account required. Completion in under 90 seconds.
Heritage design system — deep reds, aged patina, recipe-card typography — warm and specific, not generic restaurant aesthetic.

gallery.cap: Homepage hero — Butter Chicken origin claim, heritage-first visual language
Legacy timeline — 76 years, decade by decade with family photography
Menu — photo-led, with portions and heritage context per dish
Reservation flow — 4 steps, WhatsApp confirm, no account required
Mobile — story-first, thumb-friendly — designed for 83% mobile traffic
Design system — heritage warmth, modern clarity, zero generic restaurant aesthetic

outcomes.h: +57% reservations. 92% satisfaction. A 76-year story finally told.

metrics.sub: 3 months post-launch vs. phone booking baseline, same period prior year
Post-visit survey, new (first-time) visitors — net new audience acquired digitally
Post-launch with review prompts built into the post-visit WhatsApp flow
'Butter Chicken origin Mumbai' — organic, within 8 weeks of content strategy launch

quote.q: Our regulars send the website to their children and say, 'this is where I grew up eating.' And new people are booking online every single day now. Abhiraj got exactly what he asked for.
quote.a: Abhiraj Kohli, 3rd generation owner, Pritam Restaurant

reflection.h: The best brand design doesn't reinvent — it reveals what was always there.
reflection.b: Every time I was tempted to push the design toward cleaner, more minimal, more 'elevated' — the regulars pushed back. Not with words, but with their reactions: a pause before responding, a slight frown at a layout that felt too designed. They knew when something didn't feel like Pritam. The restraint that won wasn't a compromise — it was the discipline to treat the 76-year story as the entire design brief, and to treat every design decision as a question: does this serve the story, or is it about me? I'd carry that question into every heritage brand engagement after this.

title: Privacy, finally
feels effortless.
pulpy-vpn.brief: Designed Pulpy VPN end-to-end from zero — a consumer privacy app for non-technical users in India and Southeast Asia. Solved the biggest unsolved problem in the VPN category: most people know they should use one and never do, because every VPN on the market was designed for IT professionals. Shipped an 88-second onboarding, a one-tap connection state designed to feel actively protective, and a paywall strategy that delivered 3.2× trial-to-paid conversion — reaching 100K+ downloads and a 4.2★ Play Store rating within 6 months.

context.h: 31% of internet users want a VPN. Fewer than 5% use one. The product category was designed for the wrong person.
context.b: The global VPN market was growing fast, but adoption in India and Southeast Asia was disproportionately low despite high demand for streaming access and growing public WiFi safety awareness. The reason wasn't price — it was product. Every major VPN (NordVPN, ExpressVPN, Surfshark) was built for a technically confident user: protocol pickers, DNS leak test dashboards, kill switch toggles, and onboarding flows that required understanding what a VPN server actually does. The typical user in our target market — college students, freelancers, working parents — had tried one, felt confused, and uninstalled. Pulpy VPN's founding insight was sharp: the market that most needed a VPN was the exact market every VPN had designed itself away from. The brief was to build the first privacy app that a person with zero technical knowledge could use confidently in under 90 seconds.

research.h: 40 people who'd tried a VPN and quit. The reason was always the same word: 'protocol'.
research.b: I led a 4-week research sprint combining qualitative depth with quantitative pattern analysis. I ran 40 interviews across two cohorts — abandonment cases (people who downloaded and uninstalled within a week) and retention cases (current VPN users who stuck with their app). I supplemented this with a moderated usability audit of 6 leading VPN apps across 20 non-technical participants, and a large-scale review analysis of 600+ app store reviews across NordVPN, ExpressVPN, and Surfshark in India and the Philippines. The gap between the two cohorts wasn't technical ability — it was emotional experience at the moment of connection.

bullets.v: 28 abandonment cases (uninstalled within 7 days) + 12 long-term retention users — across India, Philippines, Indonesia
6 leading VPN apps tested with 20 non-technical participants — tracking confusion points, drop-off moments, emotional state
NordVPN, ExpressVPN, Surfshark — India + Southeast Asia App Store reviews coded for friction, anxiety, and praise themes
Information architecture and onboarding flow maps for 8 VPN apps — identifying the 14 decision points that caused abandonment

insights: The word 'protocol' — appearing in the first screen of every major VPN — caused 78% of non-technical users to disengage entirely. They didn't know what it meant, feared selecting the wrong option, and closed the app.

The connection state was the single highest-anxiety moment in the product: users couldn't tell if the VPN was actually working. A static 'Connected' label wasn't enough. They needed to feel protected, not informed.

Non-technical users had exactly 2 use cases for a VPN — public WiFi safety and geo-restricted streaming — and didn't identify with any of the 40+ use cases that most VPN marketing presented. The category was talking to itself.

Retention users shared one trait: a moment early in their experience where the product made them feel smart, not confused. The emotional transformation from 'I don't understand this' to 'I'm protected' was the product's most critical design moment.

personas.role: Engineering student, 21, Bangalore — frequent campus and café WiFi user
personas.quote: I downloaded NordVPN because my friend said I need it. There was a screen asking which protocol to use. I uninstalled it.
goals: Stay safe on campus and café WiFi
Access geo-restricted content
A simple on/off — nothing more

Doesn't understand 'kill switch', 'DNS leak', 'protocol' — won't guess
Fears accidentally doing something that breaks her internet

personas.name: Deshawn Reyes
personas.role: Freelance designer, 29, Manila — works remotely across coffee shops and co-working spaces
personas.quote: I need a VPN when I'm on client calls from cafés. I just want something I can turn on in 5 seconds and trust it's working.
goals: Protect client data on public networks without thinking
Reliable mid-call — no drops, no reconnects
One subscription that covers his phone and laptop
pains: Current VPN causes noticeable slowdowns
Silent disconnects during calls with no warning
Monthly billing UI feels opaque — doesn't know what he's paying for

personas.name: Meena Sharma
personas.role: Working parent, 44, Delhi — non-technical, concerned about family's online safety
personas.quote: My son said download a VPN. I downloaded one. There was too much to read. I deleted it.
goals: Understand that it's working and protecting her family
Simple enough to use without asking for help
Extend protection to her kids' phones without complexity
pains: Every VPN screen is full of jargon she doesn't recognise
No visual confirmation that protection is active
Fears accidentally changing a setting that breaks something important

problem.h: Reframed from 'build a faster VPN' to 'design the first VPN that feels like safety, not IT.'
problem.b: The original brief from the founders was competitive: more server locations, faster speeds, better pricing than NordVPN. Research made clear that this was the wrong race to run. Speed and server count were table stakes — every major VPN had them. The real gap was emotional. The category treated confidence as something users had to bring to the product. Pulpy's job was to design confidence into the product itself — to make the feeling of being protected a primary design output, not a side effect of configuration. Every technical decision had to be made for the user, not by the user.
problem.statement: How might we design a VPN that makes a completely non-technical user feel genuinely safe and confident within 90 seconds — without a single technical decision, setting choice, or jargon word standing between them and protection?

journey.h: App store to protected — in under 90 seconds, with zero technical decisions.
journey.b: I mapped the full journey from app store discovery through to paid subscription renewal. The critical insight from journey mapping: there were 14 decision points in a standard VPN onboarding flow, and every single one was a potential drop-off. My design constraint was explicit from week 1 — eliminate every required decision that wasn't name, goal (why they wanted a VPN), and the single connect tap. Everything else had to be a smart default. The paywall placement was a separate journey design challenge: end-of-trial paywalls tested poorly (felt like a deadline, triggered anxiety and churn), while mid-use paywalls placed immediately after a meaningful success moment tested 3.2× better.

phases.name: Discover
phases.pain: Category is crowded — Pulpy had no brand recognition vs. NordVPN. Discovery copy had to lead with 'simple', not 'secure'

phases.name: Onboard
tasks: Tell us why you want a VPN
phases.pain: Original 7-step onboarding had protocol selection on screen 2 — 61% of users dropped here in early testing

phases.name: Connect
phases.pain: Static 'Connected' label produced high anxiety — users weren't sure if it was working

phases.name: Use
phases.pain: Silent reconnects with no notification generated the highest-volume support ticket: 'Is my VPN still on?'

phases.name: Convert
tasks: Mid-use paywall at a success moment
phases.pain: End-of-trial paywall tested as arbitrary and punitive — users who'd had a positive experience still churned at 68%

process.h: Hard constraint: under 120 seconds. 6 onboarding tests. 8 connection animations. Shipped at 88s.
process.b: I set a measurable design constraint in the first week: onboarding must reach the 'protected' state in under 120 seconds, measured by task completion time in Maze with non-technical participants. Every design decision was evaluated against this constraint. I ran 6 rounds of onboarding testing (15 participants per round), tracked time-on-task, completion rate, and a self-reported confidence score after the connected state. Round 1 was 4 minutes 12 seconds. Round 5 was 88 seconds. The biggest single gain came from removing server selection entirely in round 2 — smart auto-selection based on the user's stated goal cut 90 seconds alone. The connection animation was the highest-ROI design artefact in the entire project — 8 iterations tested, with the version that communicated 'active scanning + protection forming' producing the highest confidence scores across all user types.

artifacts.v: Reduced from 7 screens to 3: name → goal → connect. 6 testing rounds. Shipped at 88 seconds, 94% completion rate.
Lottie animation: 'protection activating' visual with shield-forming + scanning arc. Single highest-impact design decision tested.
Goal-based auto-selection (Streaming → lowest-latency international / Safety → nearest high-trust server). Removes the hardest user decision.
4 paywall placement tests — after first successful streaming session, after 5-day streak, at trial end, and immediately post-connect. Mid-use won at 3.2× vs. trial-end.
'You are protected' persistent UI — live indicator, data encrypted counter, reconnect log, network name. Designed for anxiety reduction.
Protocol, server region, DNS settings — accessible 3 taps deep. Never shown unless actively sought. Power users satisfied; new users unaffected.

solution.h: One tap to protected. Confidence by design. Everything else stays out of the way.
solution.b: The final product was built on three non-negotiable design principles: zero required decisions (every technical choice — server, protocol, DNS — is made by the system, not the user), designed confidence (the connection state was treated as a primary emotional design brief — the animation, the persistent indicator, the 'You are protected' language were all intentional outputs), and progressive complexity (power settings exist and are complete, but are only accessed by users who actively seek them — never surfaced as default screens). Onboarding is 3 screens. The core interaction is one button. Every other screen is optional.
highlights: 3-screen onboarding: name → why you want a VPN → one-tap connect. Reaches 'protected' state in 88 seconds, no technical knowledge required.
Goal-based smart server: auto-selects optimal server based on Streaming or Safety goal — protocol, region, and DNS set automatically. Zero configuration.
'Protecting you' connection animation: 8 iterations of Lottie animation — shield forming, network scanning arc. Single highest-confidence score in all user testing.
Confidence dashboard: persistent 'You are protected' UI with live data encrypted counter, reconnect log, and network name. Designed specifically to eliminate the #1 support ticket.
Mid-use paywall: placed immediately after a meaningful success moment (first protected streaming session) — not on a countdown timer. 3.2× trial-to-paid conversion vs. trial-end placement.

gallery.cap: Onboarding — 3 screens, 88 seconds, zero technical decisions
Connection animation — 'protecting you' shield-forming state
Smart server — goal-based auto-selection, no protocol picker
Confidence dashboard — live protection status, encrypted data counter
Mid-use paywall — placed after first streaming success, not on a timer
Power mode — protocol settings hidden 3 taps deep, never default

metrics.sub: First 6 months post-launch, India + Southeast Asia
App open → first protected state. Across all tested device tiers.
Mid-use paywall vs. original end-of-trial placement in A/B test
Organic reviews — highest-rated review theme: 'simple to use'

quote.q: I've tried two other VPNs and deleted both. This one — I turned it on and it told me I was protected. I didn't have to do anything else. That's the one I'm paying for.
quote.a: Beta user, working parent, Pune — post-launch survey

reflection.h: Confidence is a design deliverable. Not a feature — a designed emotional state.
reflection.b: The most important thing I shipped on this project wasn't a screen — it was the connection animation. One Lottie file, 8 iterations, and it had more measurable impact on user retention than any feature we built. It proved something I'd believed but never had data for: on a consumer product where trust is the core value proposition, the user's emotional state at the critical moment is as important a design output as any functional screen. I now define 'emotional state design' as a formal deliverable on every consumer product I work on — what does the user feel at each key moment, and is it the intentional, correct feeling? The second learning: progressive disclosure isn't just an IA technique. On Pulpy, hiding complexity made the product feel safer — and safer products convert better. I'd apply that thinking much earlier on the next 0→1 consumer product.
